text: JAMM 121- MEDIA WRITING Spring 2017 Section 03: MW 2:30-4:20 Instructor: T.J. Tranchell Office: 303C Pitman Center Office hours: MTTh 8-12, Friday by appointment only. Email: tjtranchell@uidaho.edu NOTE: Prerequisites for this class are ENG 102 and JAMM 100—they can’t be taken at the same time as JAMM 121 without permission from JAMM department chair. (You must pass JAMM 100 and JAMM 121 with a C or better before you take any other JAMM classes.) Required text and materials: You will need the following book and access to Blackboard before the second day of class: Writing and Reporting for the Media. Bender, Davenport, Drager, Fedler. Eleventh edition (white cover) AND Appendix on style (this is an 8 ½ x 11 pamphlet available at the VandalStore. Reading a daily newspaper… Stay on top of current events. We will use an online grammar website the first few weeks of class for a comprehensive grammar and punctuation review. It is referred to as “WEB” in the weekly reading assignments section of the syllabus. Folder/binder: Keep all class assignments, quizzes and materials. You will need this material at midterm. Optional: a good dictionary and a good grammar book. Classroom policies: Attendance in this class is MANDATORY. You will write assignments and/or quizzes every day. If you fail to show up for that day’s writing assignment or quiz, or fail to submit an assignment on deadline, you will receive a “0” for that work. (One lowest writing assignment will be thrown out at the end of the term.) If you have a legitimate excuse and have contact the instructor BEFORE class, you will be allowed one make-up assignment during the course. These must be completed within a week and arranged with your instructor (make-up assignments will be supervised). If you are a student-athlete, or have other university-sanctioned absences, we will work out a schedule to complete missed work. Illness, weddings, court dates, etc., are not excused absences. Follow the procedures outlined above and I will work with you. Class begins on time. Be on time. (If you miss a quiz at the beginning, you’ll need to speak with me after class.) Electronic devices: Put them away before class begins. Same with any internet usage, unless we are looking at a specific site together. If you need accommodations for a disability, please speak with me as soon as possible and bring your paperwork for the accommodation. Important: Accuracy: you must have your facts correct, and spell all names correctly on all assignments. Factual errors and misspelled names result in an automatic 10-point reduction from your score. Revise carefully! It’s and its; they’re, their, and there; your and you’re. Learn the proper use of these words. Misuse will result in a 5-point deduction. Academic honesty is expected. We work in a world in which integrity and credibility are vital. Cheating, fabricating information and plagiarism will not be tolerated. (Each student will be given the JAMM plagiarism policy to read and sign—these will be placed in your JAMM academic file.) Readings generally pertain to that day’s assignment and should be completed by Monday of the week listed. Stay caught up and don’t skip over the examples. Learning outcomes: Incorporate news values into writing stories that are accurate, fair, balanced and complete. Select appropriate information to include in the lead and the story, and accurately attribute information from sources. Apply news style and AP style to your writing. Improve and practice writing news leads and stories that are solidly structured according to news criteria, across media platforms, and write sentences and paragraphs that are clear and concise, and free of grammatical, punctuation and spelling errors. An awareness of how cultural differences and diversity (race, gender, age, etc.) can impact different audiences, with an emphasis on writing that is sensitive to these differences. A brief introduction to the legal and ethical issues that affect news and the way it is selected and written. An introduction to social media and other platforms that inform and shape today’s media. Assessment tools: You will receive a standardized writing assessment at midterm and at the end of the term, given to students in all sections. You will be expected to write a full story incorporating the elements of a good news story. These assessments are meant to demonstrate your understanding of the news writing process: by writing a story on your own in a timed setting. These are part of your overall grade. You will write about 18-20 assignments over the semester, do a variety of short exercises, and will have quizzes from time to time, especially the first month. We live in a world of deadlines; deadlines must be met on all assignments. Late work is not accepted (see above Attendance requirements). Most assignments are written in class and the deadline is the end of class. Grading guide: A (90-100 percent): Work is clear, concise and generally free of errors in AP style, grammar and spelling. Lead is strong and copy well organized, answering all the newsworthy questions and free of editorial comment. B (80-89 percent): Adequately written copy with only minor errors. No factual errors, misquotes or misspelled names. Lead is solid and summarizes story. Fairly clear, uses proper news style and requires minimal editing. C (70-79 percent): Writing is sub-standard and requires extensive editing. Lead is weak, and/or story omits important information or lacks organization and clarity. D (60-69 percent): Writing exhibits poor organization, lack of newsworthiness and missing information throughout. Extensive editing and revision needed. Zeroes are given for missed deadlines and unexcused absences. How your grade is calculated: Points from all assignments and quizzes are added up and divided by total points possible to determine your grade. In-class writing assignments: Usually 100 points each. These will form the bulk of your grade. You will learn news writing and AP style, review grammar and practice writing through exercises provided. The goal is to learn how to write a solid news story, organize information and use proper attribution and quotes. Almost all writing exercises are done in class. This helps you learn to organize your thoughts and write on a deadline. (Expect about 20 assignments.) Quizzes: Usually 20-25 points each. These will be given frequently, and will cover important current news, grammar, AP style, and assigned readings in the textbook and grammar website. (Eight to 10 quizzes.) Check syllabus for reading assignments and stay caught up. There might be a few outside assignments and guest speakers. There are usually no extra credit opportunities in this class. If you want a good grade, attend class, do the readings and listen carefully. Be aware: There will be information in the lectures you will not receive in the readings and the examples shown in class are part of the writing feedback, so stay alert. Some materials will be posted for review on Blackboard. Good questions are always welcome. If you feel you are struggling once we start writing, come see me during my office hours or by appointment. My goal is to help you improve your writing, which is an important goal for all JAMM majors. Do not hesitate to talk to me. Tentative weekly readings and schedule: The readings and lectures the first three weeks set you up for the entire semester. They are vital. All reading listed for the week is to be done by Monday. (Readings labeled WEB refer to our grammar website.) Week 1 (Jan. 11) Readings: Chapters 1, 2, 3 Intro and overview of class, syllabus, BBLearn website and grammar website. News concepts and news judgment. Introduction to the Associated Press news style and exercises. First writing assignment: A blog about a story in the news. Week 2 (Jan. 16, 18) NO CLASS MONDAY, JAN. 16 (MLK Day) Continuation of Week 1 Week 3 (Jan. 23, 25) Readings: Chap. 4 More practice with AP style; news judgment and news writing styles. Exercises: AP Style and writing with clarity and precision, incorporating news style. The importance of grammar in writing. Week 4 (Jan. 30, Feb. 1) Readings: Chap. 7 Review, reading the news Begin writing basic news leads Week 5 (Feb. 6, 8) Readings: Review on leads (BBLearn), Chap. 9 Writing more effective leads; review of AP style. Begin inverted pyramid style (Short news stories) Week 6 (Feb. 13, 15) Readings: Chap. 10 Comparing news stories; writing more effectively. More news stories. (Make sure you are reading news every day.) Week 7 (Feb. 20, 22) NO CLASS MONDAY (Presidents’ Day) Readings: Chap. 11 How asking good questions ties to good news coverage. More writing practice. Week 8 (Feb. 27, March 1) Readings: Chap. 13, 14 Digital media, social media (with a focus on how it affected election coverage) How visual elements tie to news coverage (especially online) Week 9 (March 6, 8) Readings: Chap. 15 Mid-term writing assessment Covering speeches and meetings Week 10 SPRING RECESS (March 13-17) Week 11 (March 20, 22) Readings: Chap. 16, 18 Different kinds of news stories. Intro to public affairs reporting. Week 12 (March 27, 29) Public affairs reporting. Fact-checking and accuracy in news reports. Week 13 (April 3, 5) Readings: Comparing broadcast, online, radio and print news Week 14 (April 10, 12) Chap. 8, 17 Alternative leads and feature stories Week 15 (April 17, 19) Putting it all together: final writing assessment exercise. Week 16 (April 24, 26) Readings: Chap. 5, 6 How ethics and media law affect news and across media platforms. Opinion/PR/news: distinctions you should know. Writing blogs Week 17 (May 1, 3) Wrapping up: Media and democracy Final take-home exam due May 3 Week 18 (May 8) Finals week
